similar_scenes.name: El soul: gospel y R&B
similar_scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
similar_scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
similar_scenes.desc: El soul fue el comienzo de la síntesis de la América negra: el R&B popular con la moral del gospel, el sábado por la noche y el domingo por la mañana en uno. Lo originó en los cincuenta Ray Charles, que convirtió «My Jesus Is All the World to Me» en «I Got a Woman»; Clinton llama a «What’d I Say» el disco más funky jamás hecho. De la iglesia salieron Aretha Franklin, Sam Cooke, Al Green, Johnnie Taylor, Joe Tex, los Staple Singers, Donny Hathaway o Larry Graham. Jerry Wexler dejó a Aretha arreglar sus temas en Muscle Shoals y «Respect» (1967) se volvió la metáfora de los anhelos de todo un pueblo; con ella la reina del soul elevó toda la música negra. El mismo año salió «Cold Sweat», casi el primer groove funk, estallaron los peores disturbios y murieron Otis y Coltrane; los Impressions cantaban «We’re a Winner». Hasta «Say It Loud» (1968) el soul expresó la unidad negra; después vinieron los poetas revolucionarios (Watts Prophets, Gil Scott-Heron, Last Poets) y el black rock.

podcast.title: Community's Open Secret
podcast.body: The gospel music community had a more relaxed attitude towards homosexuality and bisexuality compared to other parts of the church, allowing relationships like that between Sister Rosetta Tharp and Marie Knight to be an "open secret." "their relationship was regarded as an open secret within the gospel music community, which had a rather more relaxed attitude to homosexuality and bisexuality than the rest of the church."

podcast.title: Component of Indie Folk
podcast.body: Gospel music is identified as one of the genres that came together in Indie Folk, contributing to its rootsy and acoustic characteristics. "This is a corner of alt rock where folk, blues, gospel, and even a little country came together."

podcast.title: Definition in Secular Context
podcast.body: Tom Bryan, author of "The Number Ones" column for StereoGum, posed questions about whether a religious song requires explicit mention of deities or denominations, or if it can simply be about imagining a better future. This highlights the fluidity of the "gospel" classification in mainstream music. "Does a religious song have to be about a specific system of beliefs? Does it have to invoke deities or denominations or holy words?"

podcast.title: Dissemination via Radio (WWII Era)
podcast.body: Gospel music, along with other styles like Boogie-Woogie, Jump Blues, Swing, and Spear Trolls, became part of a "whole new melting pot of sounds" that spread rapidly via radio during World War II. This shift was attributed to the decline of Big Bands and the American Federation of Musicians strike, creating new programming opportunities for radio stations. "Boogie-Wooogie, Jump Blues, Swing, Gospel, Spear Trolls, a whole new melting pot of sounds was created and disseminated through the radio as a result of the big band problems and the musician's strike."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Connections

podcast.title: Early Fusion with Electric Guitar
podcast.body: Sister Rosetta Tharp pioneered the combination of gospel music with electric guitar in the 1930s and 1940s, paving the way for future rock and roll artists. "Sister Rosetta Tharp, who was combining electric guitar and gospel in the 30s and 40s."

podcast.title: Foundation of Rock and Roll
podcast.body: Gospel music is one of the primary Black Music genres from which rock and roll, and subsequently alt rock, substantially descended. "It's only right, given that rock and roll is descended substantially from Black Music, the blues, rhythm and blues, jump blues, jazz, gospel, and so many other genres."

podcast.title: Genie C. Riley's Career Shift
podcast.body: By the end of the 1970s, Genie C. Riley transitioned from country to become a gospel singer, performing in full-length gowns, a shift that allowed her to take control of her image. "by the end of the decade she was a gospel singer who performed in these full-length gowns and presumably was now the person who had taken some control of her image."

podcast.title: Gesture of Honor
podcast.body: The gesture of dropping a fur coat on stage, as performed by Aretha Franklin at the 2015 Kennedy Center Honors, is a tradition borrowed from gospel music and the Black church, symbolizing respect and recognition between performers. "The media later pointed out that this was a gesture of honor borrowed from gospel music and the black church, one Queen recognizing another."

podcast.title: Gladys Presley's Favorite Quartet
podcast.body: The Blackwood Brothers were Elvis Presley's mother, Gladys Presley's, favorite gospel quartet. Elvis arranged for them to sing "Precious Memories" at her funeral in 1958, honoring her deep appreciation for the genre and the group. "At the funeral, Elvis got the Blackwood Brothers, Gladys' favourite gospel quartet, to sing precious memories."

podcast.title: Gospel-Trained R&B Vocals Revival
podcast.body: Whitney Houston's emergence in the mid-1980s was significant for "returning gospel-trained R&B vocals to the center of the hit parade," boosting the profile of artists like Aretha Franklin. "Houston was returning gospel-trained R&B vocals to the center of the hit parade."

podcast.title: Influence on Pop and Soul
podcast.body: Gospel music served as a fundamental basis for many early soul songs, with artists like Ray Charles and Sam Cork pioneering the crossover into secular music. Benny King's "Stand By Me" is a prime example of this transition, directly adapting a gospel song into a secular realm while retaining the lyrical style and concerns of apocalyptic visions, rather than just sweet love songs. "Like many early soul songs, it had its basis in gospel music."

podcast.title: Influence on Secular Music
podcast.body: Gospel-style singing profoundly influenced secular pop music, especially exemplified by Aretha Franklin, whose love songs were so infused with it that they sounded like she was "bearing witness to the Lord." "As it was, so much of her secular pop recording was already infused with gospel-style singing that, even when she was delivering love songs, it sounded like she was bearing witness to the Lord."

podcast.title: Jubilee Style
podcast.body: Before Thomas Dorsey revolutionized gospel, black singers of spiritual music often performed in a style known as "Jubilee Style," which groups like The Soul Stirrers initially employed. "The style the black singers of spiritual music sang in the period before Thomas Dorsey revolutionised gospel music."

podcast.body: Aretha Franklin's *Amazing Grace* in 1972 proved that a live gospel LP could achieve extraordinary commercial success, cracking the top 10 on the Billboard pop album chart and becoming the best-selling live gospel LP of all time. "Amazing Grace cracked the top 10 on the Billboard pop album chart, extraordinarily rare for a gospel LP"

podcast.body: The gospel charts can be topped by unexpected artists, as demonstrated by Snoop Dogg's "Bible of Love" album reaching number one in 2018. "In 2018 Snoop Dogg had a number one album on the gospel charts. It's called Bible of Love."

podcast.title: Mainstream Pop Crossover and Criticism
podcast.body: In 1968, the Edwin Hawkins Singers' "Oh Happy Day" became one of the first gospel songs to achieve pop hit status. This led to criticism from churches that disapproved of their singers profiting from hymns. "churches did not approve of their singers profiting from hints."

podcast.title: Malismal as Emotional Conveyance in Black Gospel
podcast.body: In Black Gospel music, uniquely among styles of the time, the use of malisma—singing multiple ornamented notes per syllable—was the primary method for conveying deep emotion and demonstrating being moved by the spirit. This technique became the foundation for modern impressive singing. "You see, in black gospel, and pretty much only in black gospel music at the time we're talking about, the use of Malisma was how you conveyed emotion."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 32: "I Got A Woman" by Ray Charles

podcast.title: Mid-50s Secularization Trend
podcast.body: In the mid-1950s, there was a prevalent trend where gospel-inspired performers achieved massive secular hits by simply changing a few words in gospel songs, most notably replacing "Jesus" with "baby" or similar terms. "People were having a hit by taking gospel songs and changing the word Jesus to baby or near as dammit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: More Granular Classification
podcast.body: Gospel music was identified as one of the more granular genre classifications in 1955, showing an early inclination to define specific musical styles beyond the broader categories of popular music. "You could slice certain genres into thinner slices to include big band, Dixie Land, Scott, Hillbilly, and Jazz, gospel, Broadway show music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Power Pop

podcast.title: New Form in Chicago (1940s)
podcast.body: In the 1940s, Chicago became a hub for the creation of a new form of gospel music, spearheaded by figures like Thomas Dorsey, which significantly influenced young musicians such as Sam Cooke. "Chicago which...was the city where a whole new form of gospel music was being created at that point, spearheaded by Thomas Dorsey."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: Origin and Creator
podcast.body: Modern black gospel music largely originated around the same time as big bands and was primarily created by Thomas Dorsey around 1930. He integrated popular music idioms, such as blues and jazz, with traditional Christian hymns, making it distinct from earlier forms of religious singing. "gospel music, as we talk about it now, was largely the creation of one man, Thomas Dorsey."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Professionalization Movement
podcast.body: R.H. Harris, along with Abraham Battle and Charlie Bridges, led a movement to professionalize the gospel quartet scene, which included establishing the National Quartet Convention to guide groups on appropriate conduct and appearance. "he was the joint leader of a movement to professionalise the gospel quartet movement."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Quartet Terminology
podcast.body: In both Black Gospel and White Gospel (euphemistically called Southern Gospel), the term "quartet" refers to groups that can comprise five, six, or even more members, not strictly four. "in both Black Gospel and in the White Gospel music euphemistically called Southern Gospel, the term quartet is used for groups which might have five, six, or even more people in them."

podcast.title: Root of Chicago House
podcast.body: Gospel music served as a fundamental root for Chicago House, giving it a distinct character and differentiating it from Detroit techno. "El House de Chicago tiene esos raíces en el gospel."

podcast.title: Roots in Country Music
podcast.body: Country music has historical roots deeply embedded in religious themes, though the genre also encompasses other secular topics like family and drinking. "Even country music, which has its roots deeply enmeshed in religious themes, cannot escape criticism."

podcast.title: Secular Adaptation of Lyrical Concerns
podcast.body: Unlike earlier secular reworkings of gospel songs that often required wholesale lyrical changes to fit romantic themes, "Stand By Me" was distinctive in bringing the lyrical concerns and apocalyptic style of gospel firmly into the secular realm. This approach contributed to the development of the "more gospel-inflected lyric" common in the soul music of black performers in subsequent years. "It brings the lyrical concerns and style of gospel firmly into the secular realm."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Secular Song Creation
podcast.body: The Sensational Nightingales, a highly regarded gospel group, composed a secular song titled "The Twist." Due to their religious affiliation, they were unable to perform or record this song themselves and sought another group to do so. "They couldn't sing it themselves. It was a secular song, and they were a gospel group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: The Sweetest Gift as an Example
podcast.body: The song "The Sweetest Gift," recorded by Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt, is cited as a gospel song that showcased their impressive vocal talents and collaborative harmony. "They sang together and they blew away the audience with this version of the gospel song, The Sweetest Gift, which Emmy Lou and Linda recorded for Linda's 1975 album Prisoner in disguise."
